issues.failure_explanation: The claimed counts (one prox-p evaluation per outer iteration, one prox-q evaluation per SCP inner iteration) require each subproblem to be solved by a single call to the prox of p or q. But the outer update minimizes over the ball constraint \cB(x^k,r), and each SCP subproblem minimizes q plus a quadratic over an intersection of m Euclidean balls (the constraint \bc(z,z^k)\leq 0); the paper itself only claims these are 'relatively simple' and solvable 'efficiently'. Exact solution of such constrained prox problems generally requires an iterative dual search with many prox evaluations (or a different solver entirely), so under the stated prox oracle the counts \widehat K_\epsilon and \widehat N_\epsilon are not established.

issues.failure_explanation: The lemma claims the suboptimality and distance bounds for y^\ell for all \ell\leq k whenever x^0,...,x^{k-1}\in\cX^c_\epsilon. For \ell<k this follows the standard induction: x^\ell\in\cX^c_\epsilon gives \dist(0,\partial\Psi(x^\ell))>\epsilon, so the KL level \gamma\dist(0,\partial\Psi(x^\ell))^\sigma\geq\gamma\epsilon^\sigma covers the warm-start gap F^*(x^\ell)-F(x^\ell,y^{\ell-1})\leq\gamma\epsilon^\sigma, the subsolver's input requirement h(z^0)\leq h^*+\eta is met, and Theorem thm:sub_iters applies. For the terminal index \ell=k with x^k\notin\cX^c_\epsilon, \dist(x^k,\cX_\epsilon)\leq r allows \dist(0,\partial\Psi(x^k))\leq\epsilon (e.g. x^k\in\cX_\epsilon); then the KL level \gamma\dist(0,\partial\Psi(x^k))^\sigma can be strictly smaller than the initial gap \gamma\epsilon^\sigma of z^0=y^{k-1}. The subsolver is then called outside its own input contract, Theorem thm:sub_iters is invoked outside its hypotheses (termination within \overline K_\theta and the output gap (C^{-1}\tau)^{1/\theta} are unproven), and Theorem thm:Phi_QG cannot be applied at x^k since y^k need not lie in \cL(x^k). The same gap occurs at k=0 if x^0 is already (\epsilon,r)-stationary. The deferred proof ('similar to [lu2025first, Lemma 9]') supplies no argument for this case, and none of the cited theorems covers it.
